lines.text: Coming up after the break: the hidden chemical in your takeout that could be making you sick!
MSG is an excitotoxin. It overexcites your brain cells. Literally to death.
We never use MSG in my kitchen. Never! It's poison, darling.
Every time I eat Chinese food I get headaches, my heart races... it's the MSG, you guys!
Sharing this for everyone. MSG is basically brain poison! Please read!!
For more than fifty years, three little letters have terrified diners around the world.
Restaurants hang signs promising they don't use it. Food labels proudly brag about leaving it out.
But what actually is MSG? Is it really bad for you?
And if it isn't... why does almost everyone think it is?
MSG. The most misunderstood molecule in your kitchen.
Our story begins in Tokyo, in 1908.
A chemist named Kikunae Ikeda was eating a bowl of soup made with kombu, a kind of seaweed.
He noticed a taste that wasn't sweet, or sour, or salty, or bitter. It was something else. Savory. Meaty. Deep.
So he went to his lab, boiled down huge amounts of seaweed, and found the source: a substance called glutamic acid.
He named the taste umami. Roughly: delicious taste.
To turn it into a seasoning, he paired it with sodium, making a stable, salt-like crystal. Monosodium glutamate.
Within a year, it was on sale.
Here's the thing. Glutamate isn't some strange lab-made chemical.
It's one of the most common amino acids on Earth, a building block of the proteins in every living thing.
Ripe tomatoes are full of it. So are mushrooms, soy sauce, and parmesan cheese, one of the richest sources of glutamate there is.
Human breast milk contains around ten times more free glutamate than cow's milk. Our very first meal is umami.
Your body even makes its own glutamate, every single day.
And to your body, glutamate from a tomato and glutamate from a shaker of MSG are exactly the same molecule.
So what actually happens when you eat it? That's part two.

s05_body.title: What Happens When You Eat It

lines.text: Almost all the MSG you eat never even makes it into your blood. Here's why.
So what happens when you eat it?
First, glutamate docks onto special receptors on your tongue, and sends your brain a message: this food has protein in it. Yum.
Then it reaches your gut. And this is where the scary story starts to fall apart.
The cells lining your intestines love glutamate. They burn it as fuel.
Almost all the glutamate you eat, around ninety-five percent, is used up right there in your gut, before it ever reaches your bloodstream.
And the little that slips through faces another wall: the blood-brain barrier, a tightly guarded border that controls what gets into your brain.
The glutamate on your dinner plate doesn't just stroll into your neurons.
Scientists took the claims seriously, and tested them. Again, and again.
The gold standard is a double-blind study: people get either MSG or a placebo, and nobody, not even the researchers, knows who got which.
Over and over, people who said they were sensitive to MSG reacted just as often to the fake.
Huge doses on an empty stomach caused mild, short-lived symptoms in some people. But the results weren't consistent, and nothing like that showed up with normal amounts in normal food.
Today, the US Food and Drug Administration lists MSG as generally recognized as safe, the same category as salt, sugar, and baking powder.
Here's a plot twist. MSG might actually help.
Gram for gram, it has only about a third of the sodium of table salt.
Swap some of the salt in a recipe for MSG, and you can cut the sodium in a dish noticeably, while keeping all the flavor.
So if the science is this clear, how did MSG end up with such a terrible reputation? That's part three.
Fifty years of fear around MSG started with a single letter.
So how did a seaweed seasoning become public enemy number one?
It started in 1968, with a letter.
A doctor wrote to the New England Journal of Medicine, describing numbness, weakness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States.
He wondered what might be causing it. The cooking wine? The salt? Maybe the MSG? He didn't know. It was a guess.
But the journal printed it under a catchy headline: Chinese Restaurant Syndrome.
Letters poured in. Newspapers ran with it. Almost overnight, a guess had become a diagnosis.
A year later, a scientist injected huge doses of MSG under the skin of newborn mice, and found brain damage. The headlines got even scarier.
But injecting a massive dose into a baby mouse is nothing like eating a seasoned meal. Remember: your gut eats almost all of it first.
And there was something else going on. In 1960s America, Chinese food was seen as foreign and suspicious.
Nobody blamed the tomato sauce. Nobody worried about Italian Restaurant Syndrome. The fear stuck to one cuisine, and the name said it out loud.

s09_outro.title: So... Is MSG Bad for You?

lines.text: So, is MSG bad for you?
In absurd amounts, almost anything is. Even water. But in food, the evidence says it's about as dangerous as the tomato on your pizza.
The story of MSG is really a story about how one guess, a catchy name, and a little bit of prejudice can outlive decades of science.
So the next time you see a No MSG sign, you'll know the real story.
And maybe... you'll reach for the shaker.
